name: Current Lp(a) Treatment
blurb: What can be done today while dedicated drugs are in trials.
title: Current Lp(a) Treatment
answer: No drug is approved in the United States specifically to lower Lp(a) to prevent cardiovascular events. Today's approach is to lower LDL cholesterol hard, control blood pressure, diabetes and weight, stop smoking, and in selected cases use PCSK9 inhibitors, which modestly lower Lp(a), or lipoprotein apheresis.

sections.body: Even without a dedicated drug, knowing your Lp(a) changes treatment: it can justify lower LDL targets and earlier use of preventive drugs.
sections.heading: What it means for patients

explainer:
Treating the risk is different from treating the number. Statins remain the foundation for reducing cardiovascular risk, even though they do not lower Lp(a) and can raise it slightly. Many guidelines advise lower LDL targets for people with high Lp(a) because their total risk is higher. PCSK9 inhibitors lower LDL strongly and Lp(a) by roughly a quarter, and some of their benefit in trials may come from that.

Lipoprotein apheresis, a procedure that filters lipoproteins from the blood every week or two, is used in a few countries for people with very high Lp(a) and progressive disease, but it is burdensome and its outcome evidence is limited. Niacin lowers Lp(a) but did not reduce events in trials and is not recommended for this purpose.

developments.text: The first outcome trial of a dedicated Lp(a) lowering drug, pelacarsen, did not show a reduction in cardiovascular events.
Statins do not lower Lp(a), and PCSK9 inhibitors lower it only modestly, far less than the dedicated RNA drugs in development.
